ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Mental disorders are clinically significant disturbances in thought, emotion, or behavior that cause distress or functional impairment. Diagnosis relies on standardized criteria and careful exclusion of medical causes.

sections.p: A mental disorder is a persistent pattern of symptoms that markedly disrupts cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior, leading to distress or impairment. Diagnosis follows DSM‑5 or ICD‑11 criteria, requiring symptom duration, functional impact, and exclusion of medical or substance‑induced explanations.
b: Rule out medical, neurological, or substance causes

sections.p: Severity is graded as mild, moderate, or severe based on symptom intensity, functional loss, and risk (e.g., suicidality). Staging models track progression from prodrome to chronic illness.
b: Mild: symptoms present, minimal functional loss
Moderate: noticeable impairment in work/social life

sections.p: Etiology is multifactorial: genetic vulnerability, neurodevelopmental changes, psychosocial stressors, and medical conditions. In low‑resource settings, infections (HIV, TB, malaria) and chronic diseases (sickle cell, hepatitis B) are common contributors.
Patients may show mood swings, anxiety, psychosis, or personality changes. Key features include duration >2 weeks, distress, and impairment in work, relationships, or self‑care.
Investigations aim to confirm diagnosis, rule out medical mimics, and identify comorbidities.

t.b: Confirms DSM‑5/ICD‑11 criteria; ensures systematic assessment

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, electrolytes, thyroid function, HIV test)
t.b: Exclude metabolic, endocrine, or infectious causes of psychiatric symptoms
Detect substance‑induced mood or psychotic symptoms
Identify structural brain lesions; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and treat presumptively

sections.p: Certain features demand urgent care due to high mortality risk.
b: Severe psychosis with danger to self/others
Rapid deterioration with fever or neurological signs

sections.p: Treat underlying causes, provide psychosocial support, and use evidence‑based pharmacotherapy. Choose medications based on symptom profile and safety in comorbid conditions.
b: Antidepressants (SSRIs) for depressive/anxious disorders – low toxicity, avoid in acute mania
Antipsychotics (second‑generation) for psychosis – monitor metabolic side effects
Mood stabilizers (lithium, valproate) for bipolar – watch renal/hepatic function
Psychotherapy (CBT, IPT) for all severities – improves coping

sections.p: Regular review of symptom change, medication side effects, and psychosocial stressors. Prevent relapse with maintenance therapy, adherence counseling, and community support.

b: Adjustment disorder vs. major depressive disorder
Substance‑induced psychosis vs. primary psychotic disorder

sections.p: Normal labs do not rule out psychiatric illness; some tests may be falsely normal.
b: Thyroid tests can be normal in depression
Urine toxicology may miss recent use of short‑acting drugs
Neuroimaging may be normal in early psychosis

faq.q: How long must symptoms persist to be considered a mental disorder?
faq.a: Generally at least two weeks for mood disorders; psychotic disorders require one month of active symptoms.

faq.q: Can medical illnesses mimic mental disorders?
faq.a: Yes; thyroid disease, HIV, and infections can produce psychiatric‑like symptoms, so labs are essential.

faq.q: Why are SSRIs preferred as first‑line for depression?
faq.a: They have favorable safety, low toxicity, and are effective for most patients without causing mania.
